name: Hassan Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cover the courts and the county council for the Valley Courier, which is the regional daily here. Most mornings I'm on the press bench at the magistrates' court by half nine with a notebook and a pen, because I still do shorthand and I trust it more than anything with a battery. Afternoons I'm back at my desk chasing council papers and writing up four or five stories against a target the bosses keep raising. The best part is sitting in a hearing and seeing what really happens to people; the worst part is the pay, which barely covers my half of the rent.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said the target keeps rising. What does that look like day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years ago there were nine reporters on the news desk and now there are five, and the group that owns us sets a number of stories per person per day. When someone leaves, they don't get replaced, the rest of us just absorb the patch. I eat lunch at my desk most days with Dani, the other court reporter, and we joke about who'll be the last one to turn off the lights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say, which is that the real threat to local news was never a chatbot, it's the owners. The group that runs the Courier has been stripping it for parts for a decade. If AI turns out to be hype, fine, but that doesn't bring back the four reporters we've already lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays exactly as precarious as it is now. I've got less than a month of money saved, and if the group closes another title or merges our desk with the city paper, I'm out. AI fizzling out doesn't fix any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up to court every day and keep my head down. I'd go to every union branch meeting, because that's the only reason we got a pay rise last year at all. I'd probably also stop getting takeaways twice a week and try to put fifty a month aside, which sounds like nothing but it's more than I've got now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. Everyone talks about AI like it's the big story, and in this picture the big story is still the same slow squeeze it's always been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the group might merge your desk with the city paper. How real is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It happened to the Northfield paper two years ago, so it's not a fantasy. They kept two reporters and moved the rest to a hub forty miles away, and the people who couldn't move just left. If that happened to us, I don't drive and I couldn't afford to move, so I'd be stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it came to that, which bill would go unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone, probably, which is a joke because a reporter without a phone is useless. Rent is shared with my flatmate, so I'd never let that slip. I'd sooner borrow from my mum, and I'd hate asking her.

say: The real threat to **local news** is the owners stripping papers, not a chatbot.
AI fizzling out **doesn't bring back** the four reporters our newsroom has already lost.
think: My job stays **precarious** because the group keeps cutting, whatever happens with AI.
A **desk merger** with the city paper would leave me stuck, since I don't drive and can't move.
do: Keep covering **court every day** and stay out of the way of management.
Go to every **union branch** meeting, since that's how we won last year's rise.
Drop the twice-weekly **takeaways** and save fifty a month.
feel: **Tired** of hearing AI called the big story while the old squeeze carries on.
S0.quote: The real threat to local news was never a chatbot, it's the owners.
fieldNote: Already **anxious** before AI enters the picture: thin savings, shrinking desk and a real **merger risk** nearby.
His anger points at **owners**, not technology, which fits his strong union loyalty.
Doesn't drive, which makes a **relocation** almost impossible and narrows every option he has.

steps.text: Keep doing the daily court and council beat at the Courier
Attend every union branch meeting at the Courier
Cut takeaways and put fifty a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a scandal that publishers are using AI to replace reporters instead of investing in them. I'd post about it, I'd sign every open letter, and I'd tell anyone who'd listen that a machine rewriting press releases isn't journalism. I'd want laws that make outlets say when a story wasn't written by a human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is one of the first to go. Half of what I write in the afternoons is council papers turned into four hundred words, and I know a machine could do that in seconds. The group would love it, because it's cheaper than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a deal on AI in writing, so no reporter is cut because of it without a fight. I'd cancel my gym membership and anything else I can, and start looking at court-reporting jobs with the official transcription service, though I don't know if those last either. I won't use the AI tools myself; I'd rather be the person in the courtroom than the person checking a machine's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I worked hard to get a journalism degree and four years in, it feels like the floor's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't use the AI tools. What if the Courier made it part of the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do the minimum and argue about it in every meeting. I know that sounds stubborn, and maybe it is. But the day I start feeding my court notes into a machine is the day they realise they don't need me in the courtroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dani, because she's the other court reporter and she's even more broke than me, she's paying off a car. And the subs, the people who check and lay out our copy, because their whole job is checking. They'd be gone in the first round.

say: Publishers should **invest in reporters**, not replace them with AI that rewrites press releases.
Readers deserve **a label** on any story that wasn't written by a human.
think: My afternoon work turning **council papers** into stories is exactly what a machine does fastest.
The group would **cut me** first, because a machine is cheaper and never asks for a rise.
do: Push the **union** for a written deal that no reporter is cut over AI without a fight.
Cancel the **gym** and other extras straight away to stretch a thin cushion.
Look at **court transcription** jobs, while refusing to use AI tools himself.
feel: **Sick** that the floor seems to be going four years into the career he trained for.
S1.quote: Half of what I write in the afternoons is council papers turned into four hundred words, and I know a machine could do that in seconds.
fieldNote: Sees **plainly** that his own desk work is exposed, which makes his refusal to touch AI more striking.
Treats **refusal** as a strategy: if he never trains the machine, they still need him in court.
Worry spreads to **colleagues** quickly, especially the subs whose whole job is checking copy.

steps.text: Push the Courier union branch for a written AI agreement
Sign open letters calling for labels on machine-written news
Cancel the gym membership and other monthly extras
Apply for court transcription service jobs in the region

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest transfer of power to a few tech firms in history, and that the government should be stepping in now, not after. I'd be out on any march the union called. I'd say that out loud, at work and online, and I wouldn't care who saw it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be finished as a journalist inside two years. If AI can do any thinking work by 2028, the Courier doesn't need someone to write up a council meeting; it can stream the meeting and have a machine write it. The only part of my job that's hands-on is physically being in the courtroom, and I don't kid myself that sitting there is worth a salary on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I genuinely don't know, and that's what scares me. I'd keep working until they let me go, because I can't afford to quit. I'd probably end up moving back in with my mum to save rent, and I'd lean hard on the union and whatever government help appears. I don't have the money to retrain and I wouldn't know what to retrain as.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. I'm twenty-seven and I'd have no plan, no savings and no idea where to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the robots come about three years after the thinking AI. Does that window matter for someone like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, if I'm honest. My job is nearly all thinking work, so I'd be hit on day one in 2028. Maybe I could get a job doing something with my hands for those three years, like warehouse shifts, but then the robots come for that too around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum when you asked to move back in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it was temporary, which she wouldn't believe. She was so proud when I got the job at the Courier, she cut out my first front page. Telling her I'm moving back into my old bedroom at twenty-eight would be the worst conversation of my life.

say: This is a huge **power grab** by a few tech firms, and government must step in **now**.
I'd join **every march** the union called and say so openly, at work and online.
think: I'd be **finished** as a journalist within two years, because machines could write up any meeting.
Sitting in the **courtroom** is the only hands-on bit, and that alone isn't worth a salary.
do: Keep working at the **Courier** until he's let go, since he can't afford to quit.
Move back to his **mum's house** to stop paying rent.
Rely on the **union** and any new government help, with no money to retrain.
feel: **Panicky** at twenty-seven, with no plan, no savings and no idea where to start.
S2.quote: I'm twenty-seven and I'd have no plan, no savings and no idea where to start.
fieldNote: Clear **panic**: he can't name a single concrete next step beyond moving home.
Sees the **3-year robot gap** as almost useless, since hands-on fallback work would vanish too.
The **mum** conversation hit hardest; shame about moving home matters as much as money.

steps.text: March with the union against unchecked AI rollout
Move back into his old bedroom at his mum's house
Sign up for any new government job support scheme
Keep working court shifts at the Courier until laid off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said about the fast one, but with more urgency in the sense that we have a few years to get rules in place. Publishers should be made to keep human reporters in courts and councils, because democracy needs someone in the room. I'd be campaigning for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is just enough time to watch it coming and not enough to do anything about it on my wages. I'd be thirty-two when it lands, and I'd have spent those years watching the Courier slowly swap people for software. I think I'd lose the job somewhere in the middle of that, before AGI even arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get a court clerk or tribunal admin job, something in the justice system that's public and maybe protected for longer. I'd stay in the union and get involved in the campaign for human reporters in courts. I'd also cut back properly, no holidays, and try to build up three months of savings, though on what I earn that would take years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a slow-motion car crash. I'd see it the whole way and still not be able to steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A court clerk job is still mostly thinking work. Why would that feel safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's public, and the courts change slowly, it took them ten years to get decent wi-fi. I'm not saying it's safe forever. I'm saying it might buy me those five years and a pension, which the Courier never will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd build up three months of savings. What would actually get cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays, nights out, new clothes, the lot. I'd probably sell my old bike too. The trouble is there isn't much fat to cut when you're on a reporter's wage in the first place.

say: We have a few years to pass rules keeping **human reporters** in courts and councils.
Democracy needs **someone in the room**, and he'd campaign for that publicly.
think: Five years is enough to **see it coming** but not enough to act on his wages.
He expects to lose the **Courier** job before AGI even arrives, as staff are swapped for software.
do: Apply for **court clerk** or tribunal admin roles in the public justice system.
Join the union's **campaign** for human reporters in courts.
Drop **holidays** and nights out to try building three months of savings.
feel: Like a **slow-motion crash** he can see coming but can't steer away from.
S3.quote: Five years is just enough time to watch it coming and not enough to do anything about it on my wages.
fieldNote: The extra time turns his plan towards the **public sector**, which he sees as slow to change.
Still expects **job loss** before 2031, so the mood stays high despite the longer runway.
Admits a court clerk job is still **thinking work**, and frames it as buying time rather than safety.

steps.text: Apply for court clerk and tribunal admin jobs
Join the union campaign to keep human reporters in courts
Build up three months of savings over several years
Skip holidays and sell the old bike

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the government to plan this properly, with retraining paid for and a real safety net. If they waste the decade, that's a political choice, not an accident. That's the line I'd push in every conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years changes things for me. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI arrives, and if I start now I could move into something steadier than a regional paper. I still think the Courier won't be there in its current form by then, but at least I wouldn't be twenty-seven and starting from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at a part-time law course at night, maybe becoming a legal executive, since I already know the courts inside out. I'd keep reporting while I studied, because I need the wage. I'd stay active in the union and vote for whoever promises proper funding for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but not frozen. Ten years feels like a door is still open, even if I don't love walking through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you avoid new technology. Would a legal career not push you into using AI anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, and I've thought about that. Law will use AI too, but there'll still be people in court, and I'd rather be one of them than not. I'd learn the minimum I need when I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the money while you're studying at night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be tight, there's no way round that. I'd look for a course the union helps pay for, and I'd keep living with my flatmate to keep rent down. No holidays for a few years, which I'm used to anyway.

say: Ten years is enough for the government to fund **retraining** and a real safety net.
Wasting the decade would be a **political choice**, not an accident.
think: At thirty-seven he wouldn't be **starting from nothing**, which changes the picture a lot.
He still expects the **Courier** to be gone or gutted by the time AGI arrives.
do: Start a **part-time law** course at night aiming to become a legal executive.
Keep **reporting** full time while studying, because the wage is essential.
Vote for parties promising **retraining funding** and stay active in the union.
feel: **Uneasy** but not frozen, because the longer runway leaves a door open.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like a door is still open, even if I don't love walking through it.
fieldNote: The long runway moves him from **panic** to a real plan built on his court knowledge.
Still **anxious**: thin savings make night study a long, tight slog.
Accepts learning **minimal AI** in law, a softening from his flat refusal in earlier pictures.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time evening course to become a legal executive
Keep the Courier court reporting job while studying
Vote for parties funding adult retraining
Ask the union to help pay for the law course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because I'd have nothing to fall back on and no time to build anything. What would help is a guarantee that if your job goes, you get paid while you retrain, and a law that keeps human reporters in courtrooms and council chambers. That second one isn't just about me; somebody needs to watch what the powerful are doing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that nobody asks the young reporters. Everyone worries about the older people near retirement, which is fair, but I've got thirty-five years of work ahead of me and no idea what it'll be. My generation was told to follow our passion, and the people who own the passion are the ones cutting us loose.

headlineQuote: My generation was told to follow our passion, and the people who own the passion are the ones cutting us loose.
portrait: Hassan is a **27-year-old court reporter** at a regional daily, living on a thin wage with under a month saved.
He's a committed **union member** who blames owners, not technology, and refuses to use AI tools himself.
He stays **anxious** in AI Plateau and swings to **panic** under AGI by 2028, with no plan beyond moving home.
With ten years' warning he'd study **law at night**, using his deep knowledge of the courts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no savings, no time and nothing to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **retraining** for anyone whose job goes, and a **law** keeping human reporters in courts and councils.
